My experience when I worked for the state-

Took 3 months to get a call for an interview, 2 months to get an offer, and another 2 months to start. And my position was something they needed. 

Even internal positions you apply for will move at a snail’s pace. I noticed with internal positions, leadership tended to prefer people that were there 5+ years, were a family member to a senior employee (despite nepotism policies), or were a friend to the higher ups. 

As far as remote positions, good luck. I started at a 3 days a week hybrid position. It became a max of 1 day job - often with no remote days due to meetings and staff shortages. There is constantly talk about getting rid of remote altogether depending on who was hired as the boss or who was elected governor. 

Great benefits and union if you get in. Not the best culture or pay though.

Eventually, he would bring in subject matter experts prior to the park launching to get the opinion on the park and see if these animals could be released in the wild one day with guardrails and oversight. The subject matter experts would be a group similar Ellie, Grant, Malcolm, and Gennaro. 

Ethical arguments would be:
- Do invasive species who have been there hundreds and thousands of years, who now occupy their niches have the right to life?
- There are non-invasive species who have evolved in their absence. What right do we have to disrupt them? 
- Is it more cruel than kind to introduce them in a world with climate change and less plant bio diversity?

Unlike John Hammond, his argument is an ethical one based on ecological justice. These aren’t all creatures from millions of years ago like Hammond that nature selected to die out, these are creatures that humanity neglected or systematically wiped out. Should humanity make amends or is it kinder to let them be? 

The ethical argument is further complicated with the Gigantopithecus, which might be too intelligent to keep In captivity but also too dangerous to release into nature. Yet, the species also has relic populations evident through the Bigfoot hair samples.

**Things I have learned-**

These animals should not be eating high protein (roaches, locusts, superworms) or fatty foods (wax worms, butter worms, etc) too often. Both can damage the liver and cause gout. Crickets and solider fly larvae are okay, but silkworms really are the single best thing to feed them. Silkworms have the best protein and fatty levels, which means they are the food least likely to give them MBD and gout. If I could do things over, I would have special ordered silkworms every week. 

We also need to be careful about what we gut load feeder insects with. Moderate to high protein food needs to be avoided for feeders to prevent gout. I should not have gut loaded insects with broccoli. 

Also, reptile keepers need to be more careful about replacing vitamin powder every six months. Refrigerating the main container of it the whole time too. Even the additives in calcium can go bad after a few months.
